addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

- anthropic-skills:consolidate-memory: Reflective pass over your memory files — merge duplicates, fix stale facts, prune the index.
- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx files) or Word templates (.dotx files). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, headings, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, performing find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file, use this skill. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or general coding tasks unrelated to document generation.
- anthropic-skills:explain-usage: Explain where this session's tokens went, with one simple chart in plain language. Use when the user says things like "explain my usage", "where did my tokens go", or asks for a usage breakdown.
- anthropic-skills:morning: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email or summary); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user mentions "deck," "slides," "presentation," or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. If a .pptx or .potx file needs to be opened, created, or touched, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:schedule: Create or update a scheduled task that runs automatically. Use when the user says things like "every day", "each morning", "remind me in an hour", "run this at noon", or wants to reschedule an existing task.
- anthropic-skills:setup-cowork: Guided Cowork setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a GitHub pull request; for your working diff use /code-review
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

Thanks for your time today, I really appreciated our conversation. As
discussed, I am happy to progress you to the next stage in the process
which would be a Coding Interview.

You will receive an email from coordination to schedule the interview.
Please provide your availability as instructed in that email. Once
your interview is scheduled, I will have a quick prep call to prepare you
for the technical interview.

As discussed previously I'd like to share some tips ahead for your
technical interview with Datadog. The 1 hour interview will consist on *solving
1 coding exercise - on Coderpad
<https://app.coderpad.io/login?login_challenged56d620b6a04d54a5f6ea2b4e1d912d#1171>.*

Take your time to familiarize yourself with exercise. We expect you to be
familiar with data structures such as arrays, dictionaries and sets. Also,
we expect familiarity with string manipulation. Please remember we are a
SaaS platform that receives tons of payloads as strings & time and space
complexity.

   - *Before the interview try to solve a few easy questions first* before
   getting to the trickier ones. It will help you digest the theoretical
   parts. For example, you can start with sorting algorithms. Quicksort, Merge
   sort, Insertion sort, Bubble sort, etc.
   - *Listen to the interviewer, *they are there to help you get to a
   solution, they will drop tips along the way.
   - *Never start with an optimized solution,* start with any simple
   solution that comes to your head. Once there, and only then, you can think
   about optimizations. Add complexity as you advance in the exercise.
   - *Take your time to understand the problem*, ask the interviewer for
   clarification before you start an exercise and describe your solution as
   clearly as possible. Think out loud. This will help the interviewer
   understand if you are on the right track, they will give you tips to get
   you on track if you are not.
   - *Clarifying questions is key*, lack of opinionated justification can
   also be a good indicator of seniority. Ask as many questions as you feel
   necessary to understand the context to find the most appropriate algorithm,
   describe what you intend to do before jumping into implementation, and
   describe what you are doing when you're doing it.
   - *Run your code iteratively,* don't wait for the full exercise to be
   written down to start testing your solution. You can run your code as many
   times as you need, so test any piece of
   - *It is ok to look up the docs* if you need to.
   - *Log, log and log, *as you might be lost if you find your theoretical
   solution not working. Our interviewing IDE does not support debug, so help
   yourself with log lines to see how the code is behaving.
   - *Use readable variable names, *many bugs come from confusing variable
   names, for example indexing mismatches. Expressive variable names will help
   you find your way to the end of the exercise.

Code is read many more times than it is written. Even in the tight time
constraints, we expect candidates to make sure both they and the
interviewer are able to follow the code they are writing. We expect they
also demonstrate familiarity with the language of their choice.
We do NOT expect full memorization of the standard library or relevant APIs
- if they need to Google function names, parameters, etc, as they would in
normal work that is acceptable.

Approach the exercise as if you had to solve a real-life problem with pairs
who cannot use their keyboards. Communicating will allow interviewers to
help you stay on the right track or to give you hints if necessary. You are
not supposed to need to use frameworks or libraries and reducers for
this interview, it's really about the language itself.

If you feel like it is necessary, it might be helpful to refresh your
knowledge of algorithms, time and space complexity/big O notation, data
structures and the differences between their implementations.

"Crack coding interview
<https://www.youtube.com/playlist?list=PLX6IKgS15Ue02WDPRCmYKuZicQHit9kFt>"
can be a good reference, and you can train on Leetcode.com
<http://leetcode.com/> if you feel like it!

Please let me know if you have any questions!
--

Yes — I see Maria's email, and no, the coordinator's email hasn't arrived yet.

**The email you're thinking of:** [Coding I] Datadog - Hiring Process — from Maria Seixas (Sourcer II, Technical Recruiting), Mon Aug 10, 11:44am EDT. The relevant part:

> "You will receive an email from coordination to schedule the interview. Please provide your availability as instructed in that email. Once your interview is scheduled, I will have a quick prep call to prepare you for the technical interview."

So the sequence is: coordination emails you → you send availability → interview gets scheduled → *then* Maria does a prep call.

**The coordination email is not in your mailbox.** I checked several ways:
- Everything matching "datadog" in the last 3 days, including spam and trash — only Maria's Aug 10 email.
- Anything since Aug 9 from `datadoghq.com` or the usual scheduling vendors (GoodTime, ModernLoop, Prelude, Calendly, Greenhouse) — same single result.
- Your spam folder has nothing at all from the last 5 days.

It's been about 30 hours. That's not alarming for interview coordination, but it's at the point where a nudge is reasonable — especially since Maria's prep call is gated on it. Want me to draft a short reply to her asking for a status on the coordinator? I can put it in your drafts, though you'd need to hit send yourself — the connector has no send capability.

Two other things surfaced that are on the same track, in case they're useful: Roblox sent a "Next Step: Share Your Availability" on Aug 10 and the confirmed slot came through yesterday (Fri Aug 21, 1:30–2:30pm EDT). And Capital One's Aug 10 CodeSignal reminder was followed a minute later by "Please disregard this auto email" from the same recruiter.

Also worth noting: the Datadog rejection on Jul 29 was for the *Streaming Platform* role specifically — you have two other Datadog applications still live, and Maria's process is presumably one of those.

content.text:
Here it is — a reply on the existing thread, so no new subject needed.

**To:** maria.seixas@datadoghq.com
**Subject:** Re: [Coding I] Datadog - Hiring Process

> Hi Maria,
>
> Thanks again for the update and the prep materials — very helpful.
>
> I wanted to check in since I haven't received the scheduling email from coordination yet. Is it possible it went out to a different address, or is there anything you need from me on my end to get it moving?
>
> Happy to share availability directly if that's easier. I'm flexible over the next couple of weeks and can work around whatever the interviewer's schedule looks like.
>
> Thanks!
> Devin

A few notes on the choices:

- **It gives her an easy out.** "Went to a different address" lets her check without it reading as a complaint about a delay.
- **It offers availability directly.** If coordination is backed up, she may just forward your times herself and skip a round trip.
- **It doesn't state specific dates.** You could add them, but coordination systems usually want availability in their own form, and offering times here risks them going stale. Say the word if you'd rather I put concrete windows in.

Tone-wise I matched your sent mail — you tend to be brief and warm rather than formal. If you want it even shorter, the middle two paragraphs collapse to: "Haven't gotten the scheduling email from coordination yet — anything you need from me? Happy to send availability directly."

Want me to save this to your Gmail drafts? It'll thread correctly under Maria's email, and you'd send it yourself.

The Amazon assessment email from August 6th gave a one-week deadline, putting it around August 13th, and the August 11th reminder shows it wasn't completed yet. Ritu from Audible mentioned the OA comes from noreply@mail.amazon.jobs, which makes sense since Audible is owned by Amazon—so the assessment email I received is actually for the Audible role.

The timing is telling: Ritu's email arrived just 56 seconds after the Amazon one, and she explicitly told me to disregard the automated 7-day reminder. That August 11th reminder she warned about is the one I've been seeing, but it's still outstanding. What's interesting is that despite the OA being a prerequisite, she moved forward with scheduling an interview on August 10th anyway—so there's some flexibility there, though the assessment itself remains incomplete and needs attention.

Now I'm scanning through the other companies to see what's actually pending versus what's stalled. Airbnb's assessment wrapped up on July 30th with no follow-up, Snowflake has a HackerRank sitting there, Meta and DraftKings have gone silent since mid-July and late June respectively. Snapchat's the same story. For Capital One, there's a Power Day scheduled for August 6th, but I need to verify if I actually confirmed receipt of that invitation. Bloomberg's interesting—interview was confirmed July 31st, but there was…

messages.plaintextBody:
Hello Devin,

We are excited to confirm your interview for the Senior Software Engineer - Bloomberg Product Identifier Repository position! Your interview details are outlined below; please mark this date and time in your calendar.

Interview Information:
Date: August 13, 2026
Start Time: 11:00am America/New York Eastern Time (EST/EDT)
Interview Duration: 60 minutes
Hackerrank Link: https://hr.gs/56011e0

Video Conference Information:
Zoom: Meeting ID 920 2292 8619 / Passcode 956871, URL: https://bloomberg.zoom.us/j/92022928619?pwd=OYy4aGdAJ8Z4Hvaa3EHPS0Dw2qCWz9.1

Log-In Details:

You will be using our video conference platform and HackerRank simultaneously; please ensure you have access to an Internet-connected PC or laptop for the duration of your interview.

Please log in to HackerRank with your name (no specific username is required). You may see a few lines of JavaScript as the default screen. You will be able to choose your preferred programming language for your interview (unless otherwise noted in the job description). If you prefer to use a language other than what you shared in your application, please let your interviewer know.
As you prepare for your upcoming interview, you can review some of our company and role-specific resources below:

	* [1] Bloomberg Company Overview
	* [2] Bloomberg Corporate Philanthropy
	* [3] Bloomberg Diversity & Inclusion Commitment
	* [4] Entry-Level Software Engineer Role
	* [5] Experienced Hire Software Engineer Role
	* [6] Data Science Role

As a reminder, your recruiting contact is Melanie Diaz, who can be reached at MDIAZ187@bloomberg.net. Feel free to reach out directly with any questions.

If you need to change your upcoming interview, please click [7] here. Alternatively, by clicking [8] here, you can make changes directly through your profile on our careers website.

To help you feel prepared, please visit our [9] How We Hire page, where you'll find our Expectations on Candidate Conduct, which emphasize the importance of authentic self-representation, ethical preparation, and fairness throughout the hiring process.

Discover what makes Bloomberg unique - watch our [10] podcast series for an inside look at our culture, values, and the people behind our success.

Best,
Global Talent Acquisition
Bloomberg LP

It is important to us that you are able to perform to the best of your ability during the interview process, so please let us know should you require any adjustments, and we will make every effort to provide appropriate accommodations for you.

Note: This mailbox is unmonitored and replies will not reach Bloomberg Talent Acquisition. Please reach out to your recruiting contact instead.

Bloomberg is an Equal Opportunity Employer, including disabled/veterans. To review our EEO & Accommodations policies, please click [11] here.

I went through roughly 200 job-related threads from June 11 to now. The bulk is what you described — auto-confirmations and rejections. But there are **six things with dates attached** and **several threads that have gone quiet with the ball in someone else's court**.

## Needs action in the next few days

**Bloomberg — interview tomorrow, Aug 13, 11:00am ET.** Senior SWE, Product Identifier Repository. 60 minutes, Zoom + HackerRank simultaneously (`hr.gs/56011e0`, Meeting ID 920 2292 8619). Your recruiting contact is Melanie Diaz. This was confirmed back on Jul 31, so it may have drifted out of view.

**Amazon assessment — the one-week window closes about tomorrow.** Invited Aug 6, "no later than one week from now," and a reminder landed yesterday saying it's still incomplete. It's ~2.5 hours: 100-min coding challenge, work simulation, two surveys.

Worth knowing: this is probably **Audible's** assessment, not a separate Amazon track. Ritu Vedi at Audible emailed you 56 seconds after the Amazon invite saying the OA "will be sent from noreply@mail.amazon.jobs" — and told you to disregard the automated 7-day reminder, with a new link available if it expires. So the deadline is likely softer than it reads, but the assessment itself is still outstanding.

**Shopify — Criteria assessment, still unconfirmed.** "Shopify - Assessment Invite" from DO-NOT-REPLY@criteriacorp.com arrived Aug 6. Troy's instruction: *"Please prioritize the completion of this assessment before your pairing."* Your pairing is **Mon Aug 17, 10:00–11:15am ET** with Péter Arató. I see no completion confirmation in your inbox — that's not proof you didn't do it, but nothing came back.

**Capital One — Courtney asked for an explicit acknowledgment you never sent.** The Aug 6 "Power Day Prep" email opens with *"PLEASE CONFIRM YOU HAVE RECEIVED AND READ THIS EMAIL."* Nothing went back to her. It's the final round: 1 behavioral, 2 technical, 1 case, with seven prep PDFs attached. She also asks you to email her when you finish, and promises feedback within 48 business hours.

**Roblox — Aug 21, 1:30–2:30pm ET**, confirmed yesterday. Nothing needed now.

## Stalled — you're waiting on them

| Who | Last move | Silence |
|---|---|---|
| **Audible** (Ritu Vedi) | You gave availability Aug 10, nudged Aug 11 | 2 days |
| **Airbnb** | CodeSignal completed Jul 30 | 12 days |
| **Snowflake** | HackerRank GenSWE submitted Jul 28 | 2 weeks |

The Airbnb and Snowflake ones are the notable ones — you finished a technical screen at both and heard nothing. Snowflake did reject you for a *different* role (Software Engineer - Backend) on Jul 29, which is easy to misread as the answer to the GenSWE screen. It isn't; those are separate.

Meta, Snapchat, and DraftKings are all cases where a recruiter reached out, you replied, and it died. Those are worth one nudge each — they cost nothing and you're already past the cold-outreach stage.

## Two smaller notes

**A second Capital One recruiter, Akshi Mahendru**, contacted you Jul 17 about Sr. Lead / Lead IC roles. You replied Jul 22 listing what you'd applied to and never heard back. Courtney's track seems to have superseded it, but that's a separate req family — possibly a higher band than the one you're interviewing for.

**Recruiting From Scratch (Sumit K.)** has now sent three emails about a Symmetric Health role — Jul 31, Aug 5, Aug 10. Third-party agency, healthcare data startup. Given your criteria around household names and top comp, probably a pass, but he's clearly not going to stop on his own.

---

Nothing in the last two months looks like a missed *offer* or a missed *interview*. The real exposure is the two assessments with clock pressure and Courtney's unacknowledged email. Want me to draft the Capital One confirmation and a batch of nudges for the stalled threads?

content.text:
Short answer: **no named human at either one.** Every Airbnb and Snowflake message in your mailbox came from an automated sender — `no-reply@appreview.gem.com` and `no-reply@codesignal.com` for Airbnb, `no-reply@ashbyhq.com` and `support@hackerrankforwork.com` for Snowflake. No recruiter ever signed an email to you at either company.

I'd also push back a little on the presumption.

**Airbnb.** Look at who else uses that same `appreview.gem.com` sender: your Reddit rejection (Jul 29) and your Vercel rejection (Jul 28) both came from it. That's Airbnb's rejection channel too — and it has stayed silent. On top of that, they accepted a *new* application from you on Aug 5 (Senior SWE, Content Platform), six days after you finished the assessment. Neither fact proves you passed, but a company that had scored you out would more likely have sent the form rejection than kept taking applications. Twelve days is also well within normal for a batched CodeSignal review.

**Snowflake.** The rejection you got on Jul 29 was for **Software Engineer - Backend** — a different req from the GenSWE screen you submitted Jul 28. Easy to read as the verdict; it isn't. And they've acknowledged four more applications from you since (Openflow Aug 5, Warehouse Aug 7, Cloud Efficiency Aug 10, Cortex AI FDE Aug 11), so nothing has flagged your profile.

## What I'd actually do

**Skip email, use LinkedIn.** Replying into `no-reply@` addresses is a coin flip — Ashby and Gem sometimes route replies to a real recruiting alias, but often don't, and you won't know it vanished. Find the technical recruiter attached to the req and send a short note. That's the only reliable channel here.

**One exception worth a try:** the Snowflake Ashby thread ("Initial Intake Instructions," Jul 20). Ashby frequently sets a real reply-to on those even when the From is `no-reply@`. Hit reply in Gmail and see what address populates — if it's a company domain rather than ashbyhq.com, that's a live contact.

input.prompt: How does HackerRank evaluate code quality in an assessment? What specific factors are measured?

content.content:
# HackerRank Code Quality Evaluation

HackerRank assesses code quality by analyzing adherence to best practices in **readability, maintainability, efficiency, and security**.

## Evaluation Method

The platform uses the **tech debt method**, which measures "how long it takes to fix a mistake compared to how long it took to write the code." This quantifies code quality impact across different solutions and languages.

## Measured Factors

Key evaluation areas include:

- **Code smells and formatting issues** identified through AI analysis
- **Functional correctness** via automated test cases
- **Quality metrics** such as cyclomatic complexity, code coverage, and duplication rates
- **Adherence to coding conventions**
- **Maintainability and scalability** of solutions

## Grade System

Results are categorized as:
- **Grade A**: Low tech debt, good quality
- **Grade B**: Medium tech debt, average quality
- **Grade C**: High tech debt, poor quality requiring significant fixes

**Note**: Grades only generate for candidates scoring above 50%, and this feature currently supports Coding and React questions only.

content.thinking: Now I'll put together a comprehensive answer based on the official documentation I've reviewed.

content.text:
Confirmed from HackerRank's own docs — this isn't guesswork, it's documented mechanics. Here's what's actually being scored on question two:

## Correctness is table stakes, not the differentiator

Automated test cases still gate you — you need functional correctness to pass. But since the AI assistant makes "does it run" achievable for nearly everyone, it stops being what separates candidates. That's true by design: [HackerRank explicitly says](https://support.hackerrank.com/articles/1773201418-ai-usage-summary) they're measuring "differences in problem-solving approaches and tool-usage strategies" among candidates who land at similar correctness.

## What's actually graded

**AI Fluency** — a separate score from correctness, on three axes:
- **Context quality** — how clearly you frame the problem/requirements to the assistant. Vague prompts score worse than ones that state constraints, edge cases, and what you've already ruled out.
- **Critical thinking** — do you evaluate and push back on what the AI gives you, or take it verbatim? This is explicitly "AI used as support, not a replacement for judgment."
- **Collaboration** — whether you build on earlier turns and refine iteratively, versus resetting with a fresh unrelated prompt each time.

Grades run A (strategic, clear, independent, iterative) down to C (limited, low-quality usage). There's also an NA grade for too little interaction to score — meaning under-using the assistant isn't automatically safe either; it just gets excluded rather than penalized.

**Code Quality** — separately scored via HackerRank's "tech-debt" method: how long a mistake in your code would take to fix relative to how long it took to write. This factors readability, maintainability, complexity, duplication, and convention adherence — meaning AI-generated code you pasted in without adapting to the surrounding repo's style will read worse here, even if tests pass.

Both the transcript of your AI conversation and your final diff are visible to whoever reviews the assessment — [the platform records the interaction and shows it to the evaluator](https://support.hackerrank.com/articles/9625818007-code-quality-evaluation), even though the chat itself isn't scored directly.

## Practical takeaway for you

Treat the AI assistant like a senior teammate you're pairing with, not autocomplete: state what you're trying to do and why before asking, push back or correct it when its first answer misses an edge case, and edit anything you accept so it matches the surrounding code's naming and structure rather than dropping it in verbatim. That posture is what both scoring axes are actually built to detect.

Sources: [HackerRank — AI Fluency Evaluation](https://support.hackerrank.com/articles/1773201418-ai-usage-summary), [HackerRank — Code Quality Evaluation](https://support.hackerrank.com/articles/9625818007-code-quality-evaluation), [HackerRank — AI-Assisted Tests](https://support.hackerrank.com/articles/1152916770-ai-assisted-tests)

content.text:
That specific example won't help, and it's worth explaining why rather than just waving it off.

**"I'm a senior SWE at Amazon" doesn't move the needle on either score.** Context quality is measured by whether you communicate the *problem's* requirements, constraints, and edge cases clearly — not your job title. Framing yourself as senior doesn't give the assistant information it can act on, so it doesn't produce better output, and it doesn't map to anything the grading rubric is checking. If the transcript is human-reviewed, as HackerRank says it is, a canned persona preamble in every prompt reads as scripted rather than as evidence of judgment — the opposite of what you want.

More broadly, I'll pass on optimizing for "trick the grader" rather than "do the thing being measured" — same reason as the problem-one question. HackerRank's own docs describe the AI Fluency score as trying to surface real differences in how people think through a problem with a tool; anything designed to produce the *appearance* of that without the substance is misrepresenting your ability to whoever's making the hiring call. And practically, gaming an LLM-adjacent judge with keyword stuffing or fake authority framing is a weak strategy anyway — these evaluators are generally built to be robust to exactly that pattern, so it's likely to read as noise or a red flag rather than a boosted score.

**What actually moves both scores, because they're measuring the same underlying skill:**

- **State the real constraints up front** — input size, performance requirements, what "done" looks like — not your credentials. That's what "context quality" is checking for.
- **Ask targeted, specific questions**, not "how do I solve this." E.g. "this fails when the list is empty, why" beats "fix my code."
- **Push back visibly when something's wrong.** If the AI's first suggestion misses an edge case, say so and explain why, then ask for a revision. That's literally what "critical thinking" is scored on — evaluators are looking for disagreement and correction, not agreement.
- **Build on prior turns instead of restarting.** Reference what you already established ("given the O(n) approach we just discussed, how would this change for..."). That's the "collaboration" axis.
- **Edit what you accept.** Rename variables, adjust structure to match the surrounding repo's conventions, trim anything unused. This is what actually improves your separate code-quality score, since tech-debt scoring penalizes exactly the kind of unedited AI-pasted code that doesn't fit its context.

None of this is a trick — it's just being a strong AI-pairing engineer, which is the actual thing they're hiring for at this point.

content.text:
Here's a practical workflow, building on your outline and mapped to what's actually being scored:

## Step-by-step guide

**1. Orient in the repo before opening the chat.**
Skim the file structure, look at how similar functions are named/structured, check for an existing test file. You're dropped into someone else's codebase — a few minutes here saves you from writing code that doesn't fit, and it's also fair game to ask the assistant "walk me through how this module is organized" instead of exploring blind.

**2. Restate the problem in your own words — no copy-paste.**
Type out what you're solving as if explaining it to a teammate, including any constraints (input size, performance target, what a correct output looks like). This is literally the "context quality" axis — vague prompts like "solve this" score low regardless of what you paste in.

**3. Propose your own approach first, then ask for a gut-check.**
Something like: "I'm planning to do X because Y — anything about this approach you'd flag before I start?" This is the difference between critical thinking (independent reasoning, AI as a second opinion) and outsourcing the thinking to it from the start.

**4. Ask about edge cases you've already identified, then ask what you might be missing.**
Two-part: state the edge cases you thought of yourself, *then* ask if there are others. Doing it in that order shows your own reasoning before inviting the assistant's.

**5. Build incrementally, not in one shot.**
Ask for one function or one piece of logic at a time rather than "write the whole solution." This gives you natural checkpoints to catch problems early and is what "collaboration" is scored on — iterative refinement across turns beats one big generation.

**6. Trace through every suggestion before accepting it.**
Mentally (or on paper) run it against a sample input, including one of your edge cases. If something's off, name the specific case it fails and ask for a fix — not "this is wrong."

**7. Run it, and feed back specifics, not just the error dump.**
"This throws an index error when the list has one element, here's why I think that's happening" gets a much better response than pasting a stack trace and saying "fix." It also keeps demonstrating your own diagnosis rather than delegating it.

**8. Edit what you accept.**
Rename variables to match the repo's conventions, delete anything unused, adjust structure to fit the surrounding style. This is the step people skip, and it's what the code-quality/tech-debt score is actually measuring — unedited AI output that doesn't match its context reads as low quality even when it passes tests.

**9. Do a final read-through and explain it back to yourself.**
Before you consider it done, read the whole function top to bottom and make sure you could explain every line if asked. You genuinely might be asked to in a later round, and it's your last check against shipping something you don't fully understand.

**10. If time remains, discuss tradeoffs.**
Ask about complexity or an alternative approach and note briefly why you didn't take it. Costs two minutes, reinforces that you're driving the reasoning rather than just accepting the first working answer.

## Rough time budget
With ~100 minutes split across two problems, figure something like 40–50 minutes here: orient + plan (5–8 min), build in increments (20–25 min), test/fix (10 min), polish + read-through (5 min). Leave a buffer — the repo/AI question tends to run longer than people expect on a first attempt, which is exactly why the demo test is worth doing once beforehand.

Based on the search results, here's what you need to know about the Amazon Work Simulation assessment's "select the best and worst" format:

## Format and Structure

You'll select the best (and sometimes worst) responses in a multiple-choice format. The interface uses a rating grid format where you see a list of possible actions or responses and rate each on a scale (usually "Not at all Effective" to "Extremely Effective"), and sometimes you rank options by priority. There's no single right answer to click - you're rating multiple options simultaneously.

## Scoring Methodology

The most effective response receives full marks; the least effective response earns zero; intermediate options receive partial credit. Importantly, the scoring algorithm weights the ends of the scale - correctly identifying the "Extremely Effective" and "Not at all Effective" actions will score higher than perfectly ordering the middle tier.

## Strategy for Responding

Focus your judgment on clearly identifying the best and worst options first, then place the others. If the prompt asks for the "Most Effective" action, choose the one that provides the maximum benefit to the customer or the company. If it asks for the "Least Effective" action, select the one that ignores a customer, blames a colleague, or avoids taking ownership.

## Key Context: Leadership Principles

Study Amazon's 16 Leadership Principles. They're not just buzzwords—they directly guide correct responses in the test. Every scenario tests 2–3 Leadership Principles simultaneously. The right answer must satisfy all of them.

Importantly, the scoring algorithm weights the ends of the scale - correctly identifying the "Extremely Effective" and "Not at all Effective" actions will score higher than perfectly ordering the middle tier.

## Strategy for Responding

Focus your judgment on clearly identifying the best and worst options first, then place the others. If the prompt asks for the "Most Effective" action, choose the one that provides the maximum benefit to the customer or the company. If it asks for the "Least Effective" action, select the one that ignores a customer, blames a colleague, or avoids taking ownership.

## Key Context: Leadership Principles

Study Amazon's 16 Leadership Principles. They're not just buzzwords—they directly guide correct responses in the test. Every scenario tests 2–3 Leadership Principles simultaneously. The right answer must satisfy all of them.

Amanda Halbirt

Separately, I'm noting the Capital One Power Day is confirmed for August 20, 2026.

Now I'm pulling together the full picture: today's Intuit phone screen with Lakshmi Sanam at 12:00 PM CDT (just needs to happen, flagging it was rescheduled after a prior no-show mix-up), plus a new Datadog email asking to schedule a 40-minute feedback session with Margaret O'Reilly via GoodTime link. I'm also flagging the Bloomberg interview loop invite that's gone two days without a reply on availability - that's a real gap needing action.

For LaunchDarkly, Devin flagged confusion about a mismatched rejection email six days ago with no reply since, so that's worth a follow-up nudge. Audible just got a reply today with availability dates (8/31, 9/1, 9/2), so that one's just waiting on their confirmation now.

On the confirmed/no-action side: Capital One's Power Day final round is tomorrow (Aug 20), Roblox is confirmed for Aug 21, and Datadog's coding interview already happened Aug 18 - which explains the feedback scheduling request. Shopify rejected Devin Aug 18 but he got useful feedback (the interviewer noted AI did most of the pair programming work, a signal worth remembering for next time), so that one's closed out.

For the stalled bucket, Airbnb's new CodeSignal assessment finished Aug 15 and is awaiting review, Snowflake keeps auto-rejecting with no live human thread, and Stord, TrueBiz, Meta, Snapchat, and DraftKings remain silent with no new activity found this pass. Given Devin said he's feeling overwhelmed, I want to present this as a clean, prioritized per-company list rather than dumping every dead lead - matching his emotional state by keeping it digestible.

I'm also recalling the Shopify feedback snippet noting the interviewer observed AI did most of the work during the Craft round - useful context but not an action item, so I don't need to fetch more detail on it. Now I'm ready to write the final consolidated answer with clear headers per company.

Given the overwhelm, I'll structure it as a triage: 🔴 Do today, 🟡 Needs a response this week, 🟢 On the calendar - just show up, ⚪ Waiting on them / no action. This format turns the chaos into a small, manageable set of actual to-dos, which directly addresses the feeling of being overwhelmed.

content.text:
Good news first: this list is shorter and more manageable than the volume of email suggests. Here's everything sorted by what actually needs *you* to do something, from most to least urgent.

## 🔴 Today (Wed Aug 19)

**Intuit** — Phone screen with Lakshmi Sanam, **12:00–12:15pm CDT (1:00pm ET)**, by phone. Just take the call. (Heads up: this is a reschedule — the Aug 14 slot fell through when she said she'd call and didn't, despite three follow-ups from you.)

**Datadog** — New email this morning: schedule a 40-min feedback/prep session with Margaret O'Reilly ahead of your onsite, via [this GoodTime link](https://meet.goodtime.io/w/datadoghqcom/margaret.oreilly/40-min-video/intro). This is separate from the technical interview you already did yesterday (Aug 18) — that one's done, this is the next step.

## 🟡 Needs a response this week

**Bloomberg** — You passed the first round. They're asking you to send availability for a **~2-hour virtual interview loop** plus a separate 15–20 min prep call, "allocate 2-5 hours per date." This came in **2 days ago (Aug 17)** and I don't see a reply from you yet — this is the one actual gap in your pipeline right now.

**LaunchDarkly** — Messy one: they sent a rejection Aug 13 referencing an assessment you never took, with a literal unfilled placeholder in the email ("[Feedback details here]"). You flagged the mix-up same day and got silence for **6 days**. Worth a one-line nudge to get actual clarity on where you stand.

## 🟢 On the calendar — just show up

- **Capital One Power Day** — tomorrow, **Aug 20**. Final round: 1 behavioral, 2 technical, 1 case. Prep guide and schedule were sent Aug 6; you already confirmed receipt.
- **Roblox** — **Aug 21, 1:30–2:30pm ET**, confirmed.
- **Audible/Amazon** — you just sent interview-loop availability this morning (8/31, 9/1, 9/2); ball's in their court now.

## ⚪ Recently closed, no action

- **Shopify** — rejected Aug 18. You asked for feedback and got it: the interviewer felt AI did most of the work in the pairing round. Worth keeping in mind for Bloomberg/Capital One's coding rounds.
- **Airbnb** — new CodeSignal assessment completed Aug 15, waiting to hear.
- **Snowflake** — several more auto-rejections/confirmations, nothing needing you.

---

If it'd help, I can draft the Bloomberg availability reply and a short LaunchDarkly nudge right now — those are the two actual open loops.

Thank you for your interest in Walmart Global Tech. You have an active application with us, and we’re excited to move you forward. As the first step in our process, we partner with HackerRank to deliver a standardized technical assessment designed to evaluate real-world engineering skills. As part of our selection process, completion of this assessment is required for us to continue moving forward in the interview process.

 

This approach reflects our commitment to skills-based hiring and ensures every candidate has the opportunity to demonstrate their capabilities in a consistent and practical way.

 

The assessment is designed to showcase how you approach problem-solving across core areas of software engineering. Once completed, your assessment will be reviewed by our recruiting team, and we will follow up regarding next steps.

 

The assessment includes two sections:

	Section 1: Software fundamentals: The assessment begins with a language-agnostic coding problem designed to evaluate your foundational software engineering skills.
	Section 2: Back-end development: This section focuses on back-end engineering allowing you to work in your chosen framework (Django, Spring Boot, or Node.js) with AI support to guide your problem-solving and implementation.

 

Your scores on this skills assessment may be used to identify and invite you to apply for other roles that align with your abilities. We encourage you to do your best on all sections of the assessment that are applicable.

Please click the link below to begin your assessment.

 

The assessment will expire 7 days after receiving this email. Thank you for taking the time to demonstrate your skills; we look forward to learning more about you!

 

Please note that this role is not eligible for F-1/J-1 job training or immigration sponsorship in any visa category. Please do not complete the assessment if you require sponsorship.

 

Best regards,
The Walmart Recruiting Team

The metadata-only enumeration is hitting volume limits with capped estimates needing pagination, so I should be smarter about this. Rather than brute-force enumeration, I'll target generic recruiting terms like "application," "role," "interview," and "candidate" that would appear across virtually any company's recruiting email, regardless of the specific sender.

My earlier sweep missed things because I restricted to specific company names. A broader query combining all these recruiting-related terms over the full date range, paginated completely, would give the highest recall. I should also be upfront with the user that I can't guarantee 100% completeness, even with the most thorough sweep possible.

I'll split the 60-day window into overlapping slices and run the same keyword search across each, using minimal view to keep results manageable while still capturing everything.

Actually, I already have solid coverage from June 11 through Aug 11 — that earlier sweep surfaced Amazon, Datadog, Shopify, Bloomberg, Capital One, Roblox, Audible, Airbnb, Snowflake, Stord, TrueBiz, Meta, Snapchat, DraftKings, Goldman Sachs, and more, alongside the auto-confirms. The real gaps are in the Aug 12-19 window, where I'm missing SpaceX, Astranis, Walmart, Intuit, and LaunchDarkly — so that's the window I should focus my next search on.

content.thinking:
I'm working out the timeline for this offer-negotiation plan, noting today's date and the user's ranked preferences among companies, and checking that Sept 7 falls on Labor Day 2026 since that affects scheduling.

Now I'm mapping out where each company stands in the pipeline: Roblox has a round scheduled Aug 21 but it's unclear if that's final; Datadog needs an onsite scheduled after its coding round; Audible is awaiting confirmation on loop dates right before the user's vacation; SpaceX and Astranis are both early-stage with screens pending or happening today; and Bloomberg has cleared round one and needs its final loop and prep call scheduled.

Intuit has a phone screen today and Walmart has a HackerRank assessment due by Aug 24, both still early. Capital One stands out though — its Power Day is tomorrow, Aug 20, and as the final round it could produce an offer within 48 business hours, meaning a decision deadline could hit as early as late August or early September, creating real tension since it's his least preferred option but moving fastest, likely forcing a decision before his top choices like Roblox or Bloomberg even reach offer stage.

Capital One, the least wanted option, will likely arrive first by about three weeks, creating a classic exploding offer problem. With vacation Sept 9-13 plus the Sept 7 holiday killing that week, the real window is Aug 19-Sept 4 for heavy interviewing, then a resume after Sept 14 — so the strategy is to push for compressed timelines on the top choices like Roblox, Datadog, and Bloomberg while slow-rolling Capital One without declining it outright.

Once a written Capital One offer lands, I can use it as leverage, emailing top-choice recruiters to ask for acceleration given the deadline. I should also batch the early-stage processes (SpaceX, Astranis, Intuit, Walmart) into the next two weeks so their loops land mid-to-late September, protect the vacation by telling recruiters now not to schedule anything Sept 7-13, and plan around the day job by keeping screens to quick 30-minute slots.

Looking at the PTO math, loops like Roblox, Capital One's Power Day, Audible, Datadog, and Bloomberg add up to a lot of time off that needs careful sequencing. The Capital One offer is really the clock everything else gets measured against, and since the Sept 7-13 blackout means anything not finished by Sept 4 slips to mid-September or later, that creates a tight window to work within.

I'm sketching a concrete plan for this week: handling today's Astranis and Intuit conflict, booking the Datadog session, replying to SpaceX and Bloomberg with availability that front-loads next week, and flagging the Aug 20 Capital One Power Day. I'm also noting the Audible loop lands well over 8/31-9/2, though he should give Leo Rena a heads up about the vacation so an offer doesn't arrive while he's unreachable.

Then I'm mapping out the following weeks — Walmart's assessment deadline, pushing for a Bloomberg loop and Datadog F2F, expecting the Capital One offer around Aug 25 and needing to ask for extra time, the SpaceX recruiter screen, then the Audible loop itself, followed by the Sept 7-13 blackout period and remaining decisions after Sept 14.

On Capital One timing, since the standard ask is two weeks but he has a vacation conflict, I'm thinking he should push for a decision deadline around Sept 18, framing it honestly around his travel dates — recruiters usually accommodate that.

Once the Capital One offer is in writing, he can use it to nudge Roblox, Datadog, Audible, and Bloomberg recruiters without disclosing the actual number — that's standard practice. I'm also tallying up the PTO he'll need: a full day for Capital One, a quick lunch slot for Roblox, a full day for Audible, and half-days for Datadog and Bloomberg, roughly three days total.

The bigger strategic point is not to drop Capital One or Walmart early just because they're his lowest preference — that offer is his most likely near-term win and has real leverage value even if he never accepts it, so he should keep it warm and get it in writing. Bloomberg passing round one despite him feeling "average" is also a good sign worth noting.

I'm leaning toward building a visual timeline artifact since this is a scheduling plan with concrete dates the user will want to reference repeatedly, while putting the core strategic reasoning directly in the chat response.

Chat plus an offer to build the artifact feels right since the strategic reasoning is the real value here. {"id":"1a0103923639fdb7","messages":[{"date":"2026-08-17T14:56:09Z","id":"1a0103923639fdb7","labelIds":["IMPORTANT","INBOX"],"plaintextBody":"Hi Devin,

Congratulations! You cleared are OA. Wanted to share some insight on what you can expect

I would strongly recommend visiting this link to get a feel of our expectations for the meeting. While not every topic will be discussed, this a great resource to utilize: Interview Prep<https://www.audiblecareers.com/interview-prep/software-development/the-interview>

Coding Interviews

You will have 4 live coding rounds.

  * Logic & Maintainable
  * Problem Solving
  * Data Structures & Algorithms
  * System Design

Calibration/Checklist used by interviewers

  * Is the candidate assessing problem requirements?
  * Is the candidate asking clarifying questions?
  * Is the candidate considering the treatment of edge cases?
  * Is the candidate thinking and asking about potential issues?
  * Is the candidate thinking about maintainability?
  * Is the candidate considering the tradeoffs with their decisions?
  * Is the candidate able to talk through their choice of code and decisions?

****Be sure to talk through the solution before starting coding. Discuss structuring the variables into classes and be sure to demonstrate any OOP concepts. Highly and consider variable scope/best practices whenever possible.

Four steps to ace the coding interview:

  1. Clarifying Questions: DO NOT JUMP RIGHT INTO THE CODE. SPEND THE FIRST FEW MINS ASKING CLARIFYING QUESTIONS

     * Always seek clarification about the question upon hearing it, even if you think it is clear. You might discover that you have missed something. It also lets the interviewer know that you are attentive to details. (3min)

  1. Talk through thought process:

     * Lead the conversation and explain your high-level approach to the interviewer, even if it is a naive solution. If you are stuck, consider various approaches and explain aloud why it may or may not work. Sometimes your interviewer might drop hints and lead you toward the right path. Talk about space & time complexity <http://bigocheatsheet.com/> (5min)

  1. Write clean, workable, and efficient code on the livecode (20min)

     * Make your interviewer understand your code so that they can quickly evaluate if your code does what it is supposed to and if it solves a given problem.
     * Use clear variable names and avoid names that are single letters, unless they are for iteration. However, if you are coding on a whiteboard, avoid using verbose variable names. This reduces the amount of writing you will have to do.
     * Talk about the section of the code you are currently implementing at a higher level. Explain why it is written as such, and what it is trying to achieve.
     * It’s okay to start off using pseudo code, or brute force solution but the exercise is intended for you to produce production level code, always take into consideration Object Oriented Design.
     * Review your code. Come up with small test cases and step through the code (not your algorithm) with those sample input. (5min)

Now I'm realizing Roblox's Aug 21 slot is actually just a 60-minute system design screen, not a final round — meaning there's likely a full loop still ahead, putting his top choice further from an offer than the others. Audible, by contrast, is a full-day loop with four live coding rounds plus an architecture deep dive and behavioral, requested for 8/31-9/2.

## Overall Process Structure

The Roblox software engineer interview is a structured but distinctive pipeline that typically spans four to six weeks across five stages. Candidates may have at least seven interviews before receiving an offer.

## Key Interview Stages

**1. Recruiter Screen**
A phone or Zoom call covering your background, motivations, and a check on alignment with Roblox's in-office policy and salary expectations.

**2. Online Assessment (OA)**
A multi-part assessment typically hosted on CodeSignal or HackerRank, usually running over two hours. It combines standard coding problems with proprietary game-based challenges and a situational judgment test unique to Roblox.

**3. Technical Phone Screen**
A live coding or light system design session over Zoom, usually around 60 to 90 minutes. Junior and mid-level candidates generally tackle one or two coding problems, while senior candidates often face a project deep dive or architecture discussion.

**4. Virtual Onsite Loop**
A half-day session of three to four back-to-back rounds covering advanced coding, system design, and a behavioral interview with the hiring manager. Candidates can expect 1-2 x System design (1 hour) and 1-3 Behavioral (1 hour) rounds.

**5. Bar Raiser Round**
A "Bar Raiser" interview, which is a unique feature designed to test what Roblox values most: problem-solving (in this case, system design) and behavioral skills. Your final round interview at Roblox will somewhat be like a Bar Raiser interview. It's a combination of a behavioral and system design round. They will present you with a technical problem, usually one Roblox has faced in the past, to pull you out of your comfort zone.

## System Design Focus for Senior Roles

Senior-level and Manager roles typically get a system design interview. Roblox's system design rounds come in two different styles. One is a standard system design round, and the other is a deep dive into a system you have previously designed or been involved in.

Researched all five. Two findings materially change the plan — and your Roblox guess was close but missing a stage.

## Datadog: no, F2F is not the last step

Per [interviewing.io](https://interviewing.io/datadog-interview-questions), the sequence is:

Recruiter → technical phone screen (done Aug 18) → **onsite, ~4 hrs** (2 coding, 1 system design, 1 behavioral w/ hiring manager; Staff+ swaps a coding round for a presentation) → **hiring committee** → **team matching**

Datadog runs a *centralized* process — you interview with people from various teams, and team matching happens only **after** the onsite. So there's a committee decision plus a team-matching phase between your F2F and any offer. Some reports also mention a "resume grill" project deep-dive round. Full process ~6 weeks, and interviewing.io explicitly notes it "can seem quite slow" and candidates often have to push for acceleration.

## Roblox: you're right about the shape, but there's a Bar Raiser after

Your read was: system design → virtual onsite → hiring manager. Actual sequence:

Recruiter (done) → **technical phone screen (Friday)** → **virtual onsite, 4–7 hrs** (2 coding, 1–2 system design, 1–3 behavioral — EM, director, sometimes VP) → **Bar Raiser, 1 hr** (combined system design + behavioral, deliberately outside your comfort zone)

So the hiring-manager conversation is folded into the onsite behavioral rounds rather than being a separate final step, and the actual final step is the Bar Raiser. Total **6–8 weeks**, and Roblox notably "schedules interviews far apart compared to other companies" — but candidates **can accelerate this by asking**. The onsite itself may be split across 1–2 weeks rather than one day.

## The others

- **Bloomberg** — onsite is 3–5 rounds, 45–60 min each, one day. Yours is scoped at ~2 hours, so likely 2–3 rounds — the short end. Post-onsite feedback typically 1–2 weeks, occasionally 48 hours.
- **SpaceX** — 5–8 rounds over 4–6 weeks: recruiter → technical phone screen → coding challenge → onsite of 5–7 rounds. Confirms October.
- **Astranis** — recruiter (today) → 2× 45-min virtual technical → onsite (3 technical + behavioral + department director). Four stages after today.

*Source confidence: interviewing.io is the strongest of these (real interview data). The Astranis and SpaceX details lean on prep-site content I'd hold more loosely.*

## What this changes

**Both your top two are further out than I estimated.** Roblox has two full stages left on a 6–8 week clock; Datadog has an onsite plus committee plus team matching. Neither realistically produces an offer before **late September / early October**.

I'm now sketching out a realistic week-by-week calendar to check for conflicts, since Bloomberg's likely NYC in-person round could collide with the Roblox onsite if both land in the same week alongside Audible commitments.

Week of Aug 31 needs the Audible full-day loop, Roblox onsite split across two half-days, and possibly Bloomberg NYC in-person if that's required — roughly 2.5-3 PTO days, bringing the two-week total to around 3-3.5 days, which feels manageable. If Bloomberg NYC can't fit, pushing it to Sept 14+ is fine since it's a lower priority. I'm now thinking ahead to the post-vacation week of Sept 14.

Now I'm drafting direct answers to his five specific questions: accelerate Roblox into the Audible week but not Datadog, don't make placement conditional on an offer, proceed with SpaceX/Astranis/Intuit/Walmart at normal pace (with Walmart's assessment being urgent due to its Aug 24 expiration), schedule Bloomberg for the week of Aug 24 rather than the Audible week, and address whether 4 days off is workable.

I want to flag the Walmart deadline clearly since it's only five days away. Then I'll structure the response: correct the conditional logic, answer Bloomberg directly, lay out a realistic two-week calendar instead of cramming everything into one week, address the PTO math, and specify what needs to go out today or Friday. Keeping it tight and decisive.

content.text:
Your plan is close, but two pieces of the logic need inverting — and the answer to your Bloomberg question is no.

## Correction 1: Don't make acceleration conditional on the offer

If you wait for Capital One (~Aug 25) before asking Roblox to schedule, you're requesting a 4–7 hour onsite with multiple interviewers on **four business days' notice**. Coordinators need 1–2 weeks. The ask would simply fail.

**The vacation is your justification, not the offer.** "I'm traveling Sept 9–13 and want to complete this before then" is completely sufficient, works whether or not Capital One comes through, and can go out Friday. If the offer arrives Aug 25, it *reinforces* an ask already in motion rather than starting one cold.

Same for the inverse: if you *don't* get the Capital One offer, that's when you need Roblox and Datadog most — your floor just vanished. Deferring them to post-vacation in that scenario is backwards.

## Correction 2: Accelerate Roblox, not Datadog

This is the useful asymmetry. **Roblox has one stage left** — the onsite. Pulling it forward pulls the offer forward one-for-one.

**Datadog has an onsite plus a hiring committee plus team matching.** That tail runs regardless of when the F2F happens. Cramming Datadog's onsite into Sept 2 buys you almost nothing — the offer still lands late September.

So Datadog is your natural post-vacation item. That frees up a full day in your tightest week, which directly answers your PTO concern.

## Your Bloomberg question: use the week of Aug 24, not the Audible week

Three reasons:
- It's only ~2 hours — the cheapest thing on your calendar to place
- Doing it early lets the likely NYC in-person land the week of Sept 1
- If the virtual loop is in the Audible week, the NYC trip pushes to Sept 14 minimum

Book the prep call and the loop in the same reply.

## The realistic calendar — spread over two weeks

**Week of Aug 24** *(~half a PTO day)*
- Walmart assessment — **this weekend**, it expires Mon Aug 24 at 5:58pm
- Bloomberg prep call + virtual loop (~2 hrs — long lunch or half day)
- SpaceX recruiter screen, Astranis technical rounds — 30–45 min each, lunch slots
- Capital One offer lands → extension ask → cascade emails

**Week of Aug 31** *(~2.5 PTO days)*
- Audible full-day loop (8/31, 9/1, or 9/2)
- Roblox onsite — **and here's where Roblox's habit of splitting the onsite works for you.** Two half-days (say Sept 3 + Sept 4) is far easier to hide inside a work week than one 7-hour block. Ask Mike for "completed before Sept 4," not "single block."

**Week of Sept 14** — Datadog F2F, Bloomberg NYC if needed, Intuit loop, Astranis onsite

## On the four-days-off problem

You're right that four days in one week with short notice is untenable. But that's not what this requires. Spread as above it's roughly **half a day plus two and a half days across two weeks** — and the two-and-a-half is one full day (Audible) plus two half-days (Roblox). Bloomberg's two hours can plausibly be a long lunch.

That's a meaningfully different ask to your manager than "I need next week off."

## Send today

1. **Bloomberg** — availability for the week of Aug 24, plus the prep call, plus the question about whether there's an in-person round
2. **SpaceX** — availability via the Greenhouse link (costs nothing, keeps #4 alive)
3. **Datadog** — book Margaret's session; ask her how long committee + team matching runs post-onsite

**Friday, right after your Roblox system design round** — email Mike Franchi asking to get the onsite completed before Sept 4, citing the trip. That one email is the highest-leverage thing you'll send this month.

content.text:
Book the Aug 27 slot right now — don't leave it unbooked while you think about it, because if Margaret's calendar fills you slip into September and lose more than you'd gain.

But my read is **Aug 27 is actually fine, and possibly well-placed.** Two reasons:

**It puts Datadog exactly where you want it.** A session on the 27th realistically means the F2F gets scheduled for mid-September — which is where Datadog belongs anyway. Your week of Aug 31 is already Audible plus a split Roblox onsite. Squeezing a 4-hour Datadog F2F into that week is the compression problem we just talked about, not a win.

**It lands right after the Capital One offer.** If Courtney's feedback comes ~Aug 25, you'll walk into the Aug 27 session with an offer in hand. That makes it the ideal venue for the acceleration conversation — live, with a person who's explicitly there to "help you with anything you need," rather than a cold email. That's a much better setup than having the session first and emailing about it later.

## What I'd do instead of fighting the calendar

**Book it, and add one line to the booking note:**

> Happy to take the 27th. I'm working around some competing timelines and travel Sept 9–13, so if anything opens up earlier I'd gladly take it.

Costs nothing, puts you on the cancellation list, and signals urgency without demanding anything.

**Then email Maria separately today**, because there's one input you shouldn't wait eight days for:

> Hi Maria, thanks — I've booked time with Margaret for the 27th. One quick question I can plan around in the meantime: after the F2F, roughly how long does the hiring committee and team matching process usually take? I'm coordinating a few timelines and traveling Sept 9–13, so it helps to know what to expect on the back end.

That single answer determines whether Datadog can realistically be in your decision set. If the tail is three weeks post-onsite, Datadog resolves in October and you plan around that. If it's one week, Datadog becomes worth fighting for a pre-vacation F2F. Right now you're guessing, and it's the one unknown that changes your whole PTO allocation.

Getting that answer on Aug 20 instead of Aug 27 is worth more than moving the meeting itself.

## Maria's answer overturns what I told you

Her exact words:

> "If you do all F2F interviews next week or the first of September I'm confident we can bring you to hiring committee on the same week. Hiring committee is just an internal stage and we have several of them during the week. With the current headcount should be relatively fast finding you a team to match with."

I told you Datadog's committee-plus-team-matching tail was structural, wouldn't compress, and that Datadog was therefore your natural post-vacation item. That was wrong — it came from interviewing.io's general write-up, and Maria is describing something much faster: multiple committees per week, same-week turnaround, and fast team matching because they're carrying headcount.

**Datadog moves from "late September" to potentially early September.** If the F2F happens the week of Aug 24, committee runs that same week and you could have an answer around Sept 1–4 — before your vacation, and in the same window as Audible and Bloomberg. Your #2 goes from arriving too late to matter to landing right in the decision set.

That one email you sent was the highest-value thing you did today.

## Take Friday, not tomorrow

Tomorrow is **Capital One Power Day** — four interviews, your only final round, the thing that anchors your entire leverage strategy. Margaret's session is explicitly to "share feedback" on Tuesday's coding interview. If that feedback is lukewarm, you'd be hearing it 90 minutes before the most important interview on your calendar. The downside there is much worse than the upside of gaining one day.

Friday is clean: Margaret 8:20–9:00am, Roblox system design at 1:30pm with a three-hour buffer. Just note that you also offered Bloomberg 9:00–11:30am Friday for their prep call, so Friday morning could stack — both are low-stakes conversations, so it's fine, but don't add anything else to that day.

## What to get out of the Friday call

Given what Maria just said, the ask is specific: **schedule the F2F for the week of Aug 24 — target Thursday Aug 27 or Friday Aug 28.** Margaret is the person who can make that happen, and Maria has already publicly committed to the same-week committee turnaround, so you're just holding them to a stated timeline rather than asking for a favor.

Also ask what the F2F actually consists of at your level — whether it's two coding rounds plus system design plus behavioral, or whether a presentation replaces a coding round.

## Revised shape

**Week of Aug 24** — Bloomberg virtual loop (8/25 or 8/26) + **Datadog F2F (8/27 or 8/28)** + Capital One offer arrives
**Week of Aug 31** — Audible loop (8/31–9/2) + Roblox onsite (Sept 3–4)

Three of your top four now resolve before you leave.

**The honest cost:** that's roughly 1.5 PTO days the week of Aug 24 and 2 the week after, on top of tomorrow. Around 4.5 days total, and your prep time compresses hard — Datadog F2F and Roblox onsite would be six days apart with Audible's full loop between them. That's the compression risk I flagged earlier, now real rather than hypothetical. It's worth it for three top-four shots landing before vacation, but go in knowing that's the trade.

content.thinking:
Wait, I need to catch an important detail — Audible is actually in-person in Newark, NJ on Aug 31 from 9:45am to 3:15pm ET, not virtual as I'd assumed. That means travel and hotel arrangements through Navan need to be factored in, with Audible covering the cost.

Since he's based in Glen Allen, VA, that's roughly a 350-mile trip — either a 6-hour drive or a flight — plus a 30-minute prep call with Ritu beforehand. They've also asked him to hold 9/1-9/4 as backup dates in case anything shifts.

Given Aug 31 falls on a Monday, he'd likely need to travel Sunday evening and possibly return Tuesday morning depending on flight timing, which eats into his week more than I initially planned for. This complicates my earlier scheduling draft that had Bloomberg and Datadog loops the week before, and Audible plus Roblox onsite the following week — I need to rework the timeline around this in-person commitment.

Looking at his actual prep runway now, it's packed: Capital One Power Day, Roblox system design, the Bloomberg loop, and Datadog F2F all land in the same window before Audible's four-round loop, which is the most technically demanding of the bunch. One option worth considering is asking Audible to push to 9/3 or 9/4 instead, since Rena indicated those dates are still being held as alternatives — that would buy him a couple more days of breathing room.

But that risks colliding with the Roblox onsite window on Sept 3-4. A better move might be shifting Datadog's F2F to the week of Aug 31 instead of Aug 27-28, since Maria indicated committee could still convene that same week for early September — this would free up the week of Aug 24 entirely for Audible prep.

Still, neither option is clean: one crowds Aug 24-28 with Bloomberg and Datadog leaving no Audible prep time, while the other crowds the week of Aug 31 with Audible, Datadog, and possibly Roblox all together. I'm trying to pin down when Roblox's onsite would realistically land given the Friday Aug 21 system design round and typical one-week feedback turnaround — it's likely early September or the week of Sept 14.

I could try asking Audible to shift to Sept 2 or 3, which would free up dedicated prep time before Aug 31, but that risks pushing Roblox further out and probably isn't necessary anyway since Roblox likely can't happen before Sept 3 given the screen timeline. Really, Aug 31 was his own first choice and they accommodated it, so reopening that now feels like the wrong move.

Counting actual prep days, he has evenings plus the Aug 22-23 weekend and Aug 29-30 free around his other interviews, which isn't nothing — and the Audible content overlaps heavily with what he's already prepping for Datadog and Roblox, so there's real synergy across the system design and DS&A prep.

The real issue isn't content readiness but logistics: it's in-person in Newark (travel Sunday, full day Monday 9:45-3:15 with four interviews), he needs to book through Navan soon before flights get pricier, schedule a 30-min prep call with Ritu, and note they're holding 9/1-9/4 as a backup in case things shift. Leaning toward recommending he keep Aug 31.

I consider moving Datadog F2F to Sept 2-4 since Maria said that window works, but that risks colliding with a potential Roblox onsite in the same window. Really the core problem is fitting four major events — Bloomberg loop, Datadog F2F, Audible loop, Roblox onsite — into roughly 10 business days between Aug 24 and Sept 4, which is tight but workable if spread out: Bloomberg on the 25th or 26th, Datadog F2F on the 27th or 28th, and so on.

Keeping Datadog at Aug 27-28 and Audible at Aug 31 actually works fine — the real issue is prep density, not a scheduling conflict, with the weekend of Aug 22-23 serving as the main Audible prep block. Since both Datadog and Audible are system-design-heavy, having only a few days and one travel day between them means prep will compound, so I should flag that he confirm with Rena whether her "hold these dates" request is locked in or still flexible.

As for whether to push Audible later for more prep time — Sept 3-4 collides with Roblox, so Aug 31 is really the most defensible date, though Sept 2 could be worth asking for if he wants a bit more breathing room.
